title: State of the State Courts 2025: Public Opinion Poll Findings
pub: National Center for State Courts (survey by GBAO Strategies for the CCJ/COSCA Public Engagement, Trust and Confidence committee)
author: National Center for State Courts · GBAO Strategies

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports selective, responsibly governed court deployment rather than either blanket adoption or rejection. Its national survey adds public-confidence evidence: respondents more often expect uncaught AI mistakes to harm trust than expect efficiency gains, while NCSC still advocates responsible adoption and institutional leadership. It does not independently establish jagged capability or task-level performance.
qs: As news about fake evidence and hallucinations in briefs and opinions spreads, a majority think that AI will be more harmful than helpful to our courts.
This presents courts with both practical and PR challenges as they move to adopt AI responsibly.

kp.k: Survey measures national registered-voter opinion, not AI performance
kp.d: GBAO Strategies conducted NCSC’s online survey of 1,000 registered voters on November 12-16, 2025. The slide deck reports a margin of error of +/= 3.1% (19 times out of 20), while the findings page describes about 3%. Representative sampling provides a national snapshot, not individual-state conclusions. The AI findings concern respondents’ expectations of court AI, rather than measured effects of deployment.
qs: This year's survey was conducted online between November 12-16, 2025.
We surveyed 1,000 registered voters, which provides a margin of error of about 3%, 19 times out of 20.
The sample provides a national snapshot of opinion, but does not allow us to draw conclusions at the level of any individual state.

kp.k: More respondents expect AI harm than court efficiency gains
kp.d: Figure 6 reports that 51% select the statement that AI will hurt state courts through mistakes judges and staff cannot always catch and diminished trust in decisions; 31% select the statement that AI will improve speed and efficiency through less paperwork, reduced backlogs and better case-management tools; 18% do not know. These are responses to competing prospective statements, not findings that either outcome has occurred.
qs: Courts face a daunting challenge in convincing Americans that AI will make the justice system better.
As news about fake evidence and hallucinations in briefs and opinions spreads, a majority think that AI will be more harmful than helpful to our courts.

kp.k: Responsible court AI adoption requires public-facing leadership
kp.d: NCSC interprets public skepticism as creating both practical and public-relations challenges for courts adopting AI responsibly. It recommends that courts demonstrate leadership on AI; the document does not establish that a particular adoption or communication strategy improves public trust.
qs: This presents courts with both practical and PR challenges as they move to adopt AI responsibly.
This finding emphasizes how critical it is for courts to demonstrate leadership on AI.

kp.k: State-court confidence remains stable and comparatively high
kp.d: The survey reports 62% expressing a great deal or some confidence in state courts in 2025, compared with 63% in 2024 and 61% in 2023. Figure 1 places state courts above state legislatures (59%), governors (57%), federal courts (52%) and the U.S. Supreme Court (51%). NCSC characterizes overall state-court trust as stable despite concerns about equal justice and AI.
qs: This year's survey finds that 62% of respondents express a great deal or some trust in our state court system.
Last year's survey placed that number at 63%, and the 2023 figure was 61%, suggesting that public trust in state courts is stable.

kp.k: Equal-justice perceptions deteriorate despite stable overall trust
kp.d: The findings page reports that the share agreeing state courts provide equal justice declined from 62% in 2014 to 44% in 2025. Figure 2 reports 50% rating courts not well or not at all well on equal justice in 2025. Separately, the page attributes concerns about politics, money, racial bias, cost and complexity to recent qualitative research, rather than presenting these as experimentally established causes.
qs: The percentage of Americans agreeing that state courts provide equal justice has slipped from 62% in 2014 to 44% this year.
has revealed that Americans are concerned that politics, money, racial bias, and the cost and complexity of court all contribute to this trust gap.

kp.k: Community disconnection reinforces calls for judicial engagement
kp.d: In Figure 3, 45% select the view that too many judges do not understand court users’ challenges and should listen more in the community; 41% select the view that judges reflect community values and understand those challenges; 14% do not know. NCSC frames community engagement as a response to these concerns.
qs: But rising concerns about a two-tiered justice system, distrust of AI, and barriers from complex, costly processes are driving calls for greater community engagement as well as legal education reform.

kp.k: Younger voters view state courts more favorably
kp.d: Figure 4 compares voters aged 18-29 with respondents overall: fair and impartial, 53% versus 50%; innovative, 42% versus 33%; transparent and accountable, 47% versus 41%; hardworking, 64% versus 55%. The document describes younger voters as more optimistic about state courts; these measures are not age-specific findings about AI acceptance.
qs: The 18-29 age cohort is considerably sunnier in its views of state courts than any other age group.

Generation Z voters are three points more likely to agree that state courts are fair and impartial; six points more likely to agree that state courts are transparent and accountable; and nine points more likely to agree that state courts are both innovative and hardworking.

kp.k: Court complexity and legal costs dominate access concerns
kp.d: Figure 9 reports perceived access problems: uncertainty about court expectations or process information, 80%; not knowing where to obtain legal help, 76%; confusing forms and paperwork, 76%; appearing without a lawyer because of unaffordability, 74%; and insufficient local lawyers, 48%. Unaffordable representation receives the highest very-problematic rating, 41%. These are public assessments of barriers, not measured prevalence of unmet legal need.
qs: The complexity of court processes and the cost of legal assistance rise to the top of concerns about our access to justice crisis.

kp.k: Public supports practical legal education reforms for access
kp.d: Figure 10 reports that respondents consider three reforms very or somewhat effective in improving access to legal-system support: more law-school training for everyday legal problems, 74%; more supervised in-court experience for students and new graduates, 74%; and bar examinations better measuring real-world skills, 66%. These are expectations of effectiveness, not evaluated reform outcomes or specifically AI-training proposals.
qs: Most people see reforming legal education as an effective part of the solution.

Two-thirds or more believe that legal education reforms like encouraging law schools to do more to train lawyers to handle everyday legal problems, allowing law students and new law graduates more in-court supervised experience, and updating the bar exam to better measure real-world skills would all be effective in helping close the access gap.

kp.k: Personal networks lead trust in court information
kp.d: Figure 5 reports a great deal or some trust in information from family, friends, neighbors or co-workers at 76%; local newspapers and their websites and state-court websites each at 68%; churches or other community groups at 58%; local elected officials at 49%; state-court social media at 44%; and respondents’ own social-media accounts at 35%. These findings describe trusted information channels, not tested interventions for communicating about AI.
qs: Percent saying they put a great deal or some trust in the information source.

kp.k: Judicial security legislation attracts broad public support
kp.d: Half of respondents believe threats of politically motivated violence against elected officials, judges and other public officials increased over the previous year; Figure 7 reports 67% among those aged 65 and older. Figure 8 reports 32% strongly supporting and 46% somewhat supporting proposed legislation establishing a State Judicial Threat Intelligence and Resource Center, versus 4% strongly opposed, 8% somewhat opposed and 10% unsure. These findings concern perceived threats and legislative preferences, not documented changes in violence.
qs: with 50% of those surveyed indicating they think threats have increased in the last 12 months.
that would help protect state court judges and court staff has overwhelming public support.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: NCSC reports that the public predominantly anticipates harmful rather than beneficial effects from AI in state courts, creating practical and public-confidence challenges for adoption.
pts.d: In Figure 6, 51% selected the survey statement anticipating increased mistakes that judges and staff might not catch and diminished trust in court decisions; 31% selected the statement anticipating faster, more efficient courts through reduced paperwork, smaller backlogs and better case-management tools; 18% answered 'Don’t Know'. These are respondent preferences between survey-provided predictions, not demonstrated effects of AI or unconditional predictions endorsed by NCSC. NCSC itself concludes that courts face a substantial challenge in convincing the public that AI will improve justice and stresses leadership in responsible adoption.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence is a national registered-voter opinion survey, rather than measurement of AI accuracy, productivity or actual court outcomes.
pts.d: GBAO Strategies conducted the NCSC online survey of 1,000 registered voters on November 12–16, 2025. The slide deck reports a margin of error of ±3.1%, 19 times out of 20; the findings page rounds this to about 3%. Figure 6 supplies the 51% harmful, 31% helpful and 18% uncertain distribution. NCSC describes representative sampling and explicitly excludes state-level inference. References to fake evidence and hallucinations provide context, but the supplied material identifies no particular incidents, measured error rates or causal evidence that such news produced the reported attitudes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings describe November 2025 attitudes toward prospective AI adoption, without a forecast deadline or a specified deployment model.
pts.d: The opinion snapshot is dated November 12–16, 2025. The anticipated benefits and harms concern future AI use in state courts, but the source gives no timeframe for their realization and does not distinguish particular models, tasks or levels of autonomy. The harmful scenario includes limits to human detection of mistakes; the beneficial scenario concerns administrative efficiency and case management. NCSC frames the institutional challenge as arising while courts move toward responsible adoption. Although the document includes a teaser describing support for access-improving AI tools in the 2024 report, it does not provide comparable question wording or figures sufficient to establish a quantified year-on-year change.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern state courts, judges, court staff and the public relying on court decisions.
pts.d: The survey's harmful scenario concerns judges' and staff members' ability to catch mistakes and the public's trust in decisions. Its beneficial scenario concerns court administration, paperwork, backlogs and judges' case-management capabilities. NCSC's own interpretation places responsibility on court leadership to address practical adoption issues and public confidence. The measured population is registered voters nationally, not specifically court users or legal practitioners. The source does not make AI-related predictions about law-firm staffing, fees, legal-provider competition or lawyer displacement, and its separate access-to-justice and legal-education findings should not be treated as evidence of AI's effects.
